items.title: Why the three-month plan starts with integration tests
items.body:
The critique's plan is ordered, and item 1 is: "Add integration tests around login, PTO visibility, approval authorization, and audit logging." The reason is in its risk table: there are no automated tests at all, while critical authorization logic lives in `Program.cs`. Any refactor or new feature could silently break who may approve what. Tests that pin today's behaviour make every later change safer. That is why refactoring `Program.cs` is item 3 and comes "only where tests demand it".

Why the others are wrong:
- Pagination is item 5, near the end.
- Full-text search is not in the plan; slow search is listed only as a hypothesis to measure.
- Splitting `Program.cs` is item 3, after tests and migrations.

excerpts.quote: 1. Add integration tests around login, PTO visibility, approval authorization, and audit logging. 2. Add migrations and replace `EnsureCreatedAsync`. 3. Split `Program.cs` into endpoint groups plus small services only where tests demand it. 4. Add structured logging and health checks beyond `/api/health` in [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L68-L68). 5. Add pagination and resource-specific permission policy helpers.
| High | No automated tests | No test projects found; critical auth logic in [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L342-L353). | Add API integration tests first. |

items.title: What the critique recommends for the committed JWT key
items.body:
`appsettings.json` contains a JWT signing key in plain text: "replace-this-development-key-with-a-secret-at-least-32-chars". Anyone with that key can create tokens the API will accept, so it must never be the key outside development. The critique rates this High and recommends: "Move secrets to user-secrets/env for non-dev." That means the key comes from the .NET user-secrets store on a developer machine, or from environment configuration in other environments, never from a file committed to git.

Why the others are wrong:
- Rotating on every start would invalidate all tokens on each restart and is not the recommendation.
- Switching to cookies does not address where the secret lives.
- A shorter key is *weaker*, not stronger.

excerpts.quote: "Jwt": { "Issuer": "Nethris.Api", "Audience": "Nethris.Client", "Key": "replace-this-development-key-with-a-secret-at-least-32-chars" },
| High | Development JWT key in config | [appsettings.json](../../../server/Nethris.Api/appsettings.json#L5-L9) | Move secrets to user-secrets/env for non-dev. |

items.title: What a senior asks about a hidden Approvals tab
items.body:
Hiding a tab only changes what the browser *shows*. The server endpoint still exists, and anyone with a token can send a request to it directly with curl, a script or the browser's dev tools. So the only question that matters is what the server does with that request. The guide's table: junior says "The Approvals tab is hidden."; senior asks "What happens if the user posts directly to the endpoint?" The layers table makes the same point: the React UI must not own final authorization.

Why the others are wrong:
- Whether it reappears after refresh is still about the UI.
- CSS versus DOM removal is still about the UI.
- Mobile breakpoints are still about the UI.
All three test hiding, not protection.

excerpts.quote: | "The Approvals tab is hidden." | "What happens if the user posts directly to the endpoint?" |
| React UI | Rendering, local form state, role-aware visibility | Final authorization, persistence invariants |

items.title: What stops a repeated approval from deducting twice
items.body:
The decision handler first checks the request's status: `if (pto.Status is PtoStatus.Approved or PtoStatus.Rejected or PtoStatus.Cancelled)` it returns 409 Conflict, "This PTO request is already closed." The first approval sets the status to Approved and deducts the balance. A repeated call finds the request closed and stops before any deduction. The guide lists this as its idempotency protection: repeated approval calls "should not double-deduct balance", and the current guard is this closed-state check.

Why the others are wrong:
- Disabling a button is UI-only; the server must protect itself.
- There is no idempotency key in this code.
- No unique index on the audit log is described; the protection is the status check.

excerpts.quote: if (pto.Status is PtoStatus.Approved or PtoStatus.Rejected or PtoStatus.Cancelled) { return Results.Conflict(new { message = "This PTO request is already closed." }); }
- Idempotency: repeated approval calls should not double-deduct balance. Current closed-state guard is [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L337-L340).

items.title: Start here: the Nethris HRIS upskill lab and where to begin
items.body:
Nethris is a small HR app: an employee directory plus a paid-time-off (PTO) request and approval workflow. The server is an ASP.NET Core minimal API (almost everything is in `server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs`) with EF Core over SQLite; the client is React. The training material is in `docs/upskill/`.

Read in this order:

- **docs/upskill/README.md**: what the lab is, its timeboxed paths and its conventions.
- **01-codebase-cartography/**: the system map, a file reading order and the key flows (trace the PTO flow).
- **03-architecture-and-patterns/**: boundaries and layers, the data model, validation and permissions, side effects and reliability, and the architecture critique. Most quizzes in this pack come from this folder.
- **02-stack-and-language-mastery/** and **04-code-reading-gym/** for depth.

Every code claim in these docs links to a file and line range (for example `Program.cs#L342-L353`). Follow the link and read the lines before you trust the claim.

excerpts.quote: Nethris is a compact employee directory and PTO workflow app

Senior mindset: a junior asks "how do I make it work?", a mid-level engineer asks "is this the right pattern?", and a senior asks "what does this commit us to, who pays for it, and how do we reduce risk?"

readMore.why: The suggested order for reading the source files.
The PTO request and approval flow, traced.

items.title: How the PTO approval saves balance and audit together
items.body:
In the decision handler, the HR/Admin branch sets `pto.Status = PtoStatus.Approved` and subtracts the hours from `pto.Employee.PtoBalanceHours`. These are changes to tracked entities, still only in memory. Then `db.AuditLogs.Add(...)` adds the audit row, and a single `await db.SaveChangesAsync()` writes everything. EF Core runs one SaveChanges as one transaction, so either both the balance change and the audit row are saved, or neither is. The reliability table: "Balance update and audit save together."

Why the others are wrong:
- The balance is really deducted and stored, not recomputed on read.
- There is no separate transaction for the audit entry.
- There is no background job; the guide found none.

excerpts.quote: pto.Status = PtoStatus.Approved; if (pto.Employee is not null) { pto.Employee.PtoBalanceHours -= pto.Hours; }
db.AuditLogs.Add(Audit(principal, request.Decision.ToString(), nameof(PtoRequest), pto.Id.ToString(), pto.Status.ToString())); await db.SaveChangesAsync();
| PTO decision audit and balance update | [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L367-L381) | Balance update and audit save together. |

items.title: Concept: confirmed findings, hypotheses, and design boundaries
items.body:
The lab is strict about how sure a claim is. Its README conventions: every codebase claim includes a path and line anchor; "illustrative fake code" means the snippet is not in this repo; "investigate" means there is evidence, but no failing test or reproduction has been verified.

The architecture critique applies the same discipline. It sorts its points into *confirmed* facts (things you can check by looking, such as whether a folder exists) and *hypotheses* (things that might be a problem but need evidence first). It also has a prioritised risk table and an ordered plan for "If I Owned This For Three Months".

Two habits to take from this. First, a missing feature is not automatically a bug: sometimes the docs call it a deliberate boundary of the current design. Second, when you review code, label your own claims the same way. "This is broken" and "this might be slow" deserve different evidence before anyone acts on them.

excerpts.quote: - Every codebase claim should include a path and line anchor. - "Illustrative fake code" means the snippet is not in this repo. - "Investigate" means evidence exists, but no failing test or runtime reproduction was verified.
## Confirmed Vs Hypothesis

readMore.why: The full critique: strengths, risks, plan and confirmed vs hypothesis.
The running register of known risks.

items.title: How the IDOR checklist treats the open employee profile
items.body:
**IDOR** (insecure direct object reference) means a user changes an id in a request to reach a resource they do not own. The checklist notes that `GET /api/employees/{id}` lets any signed-in user fetch any employee profile. The code confirms it: the endpoint only has `.RequireAuthorization()` and looks the employee up by id with no visibility filter. But the checklist does not call it a bug. It says: "This may be intended for a directory." In many companies everyone may see a colleague's profile; whether this one should be visible is a product decision to confirm. The PTO list is treated differently because it really does filter by employee and manager.

Why the others are wrong:
- The PTO list *is* filtered, so the two are not equivalent.
- Random ids do not make an endpoint safe; ids leak and can be shared.
- The doc does not call it a confirmed IDOR or prescribe 404.

excerpts.quote: IDOR means insecure direct object reference: a user manipulates an id to access or modify a resource they do not own. - `GET /api/employees/{id}` allows any authenticated user to fetch any employee profile [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L149-L153). This may be intended for a directory.

app.MapGet("/api/employees/{id:guid}", async (Guid id, HrisDbContext db) => { var employee = await EmployeeIncludes(db.Employees).SingleOrDefaultAsync(e => e.Id == id); return employee is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(ToEmployeeResponse(employee)); }).RequireAuthorization();

items.title: Concept: what each layer owns, and what it must not own
items.body:
01-boundaries-and-layers.md has a table with three useful columns: what each layer **owns**, what it **must not own**, and the evidence.

- The **React UI** renders screens and holds form state. It may hide or show things by role, but it must not be the final word on who is allowed to do something.
- The **client API** module sends HTTP requests with the token.
- The **minimal API** in `Program.cs` binds requests, checks auth and runs the workflow.
- **Domain entities** describe data shapes.
- **EF Core** (`HrisDbContext.cs`) defines relationships, indexes and what happens on delete.

Use the table as a checklist when reading a quiz. If a claim says "the UI handles it", ask whether that layer is allowed to own it. If it is about deleting related rows, the answer lives in the EF configuration. If it is about who may approve, it lives in the endpoint code in `Program.cs`.

excerpts.quote: | Layer | Owns | Must not own | Evidence |
| Minimal API | Request binding, auth checks, orchestration, mapping | Long-term domain complexity if it grows | [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L70-L395) |

items.title: What DeleteBehavior.Restrict on Employee to Manager prevents
items.body:
The manager relationship is configured with `.OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)`. Restrict means: you cannot delete a row while other rows still point at it. A manager with direct reports cannot be deleted until those reports are reassigned. The alternative, Cascade, would delete the dependents along with the manager, and their dependents, all the way down the org chart. The data-model guide: "Restrict delete avoids cascading through org tree."

Why the others are wrong:
- Restrict is about deletes, not about changing a manager after hire.
- It does not check whether an employee is their own manager.
- Loading related data (`Include`) is a query concern, unrelated to delete behaviour.

excerpts.quote: entity.HasOne(e => e.Manager) .WithMany(e => e.DirectReports) .HasForeignKey(e => e.ManagerId) .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict);
| Employee -> Manager/direct reports | [HrisDbContext.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Data/HrisDbContext.cs#L23-L26) | Restrict delete avoids cascading through org tree. |

items.title: The two resource checks that make a manager's decision Forbid
items.body:
The endpoint's role policy only says "is this user an approver at all?". Inside the handler come two resource-level checks, both for the Manager role:

- `isManagerForEmployee` compares `pto.Employee?.ManagerId` with the approver's employee id. If the manager is not the employee's direct manager, the result is `Forbid()`.
- If `pto.Status == PtoStatus.PendingHr`, the request is already waiting for HR's final approval, and a manager gets `Forbid()`.

The validation guide lists exactly these two: the direct manager check, and "Manager blocked from HR-stage final approval".

Why the others are wrong:
- Holidays and start dates are not checked here.
- Policies are checked before the handler, and balance is not a Forbid reason.
- Token age and department are not part of these checks.

excerpts.quote: var isManagerForEmployee = pto.Employee?.ManagerId == approverId; if (role == SecurityRole.Manager && !isManagerForEmployee) { return Results.Forbid(); } if (role == SecurityRole.Manager && pto.Status == PtoStatus.PendingHr) { return Results.Forbid();

Resource-level checks happen inside PTO decision: - Direct manager check in [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L342-L348). - Manager blocked from HR-stage final approval in [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L350-L353).

items.title: Why EnsureCreatedAsync blocks schema changes on existing data
items.body:
`EnsureCreatedAsync` creates the database and its tables only if the database does not exist yet. If it exists, it does nothing: it does not compare the model with the tables or add new columns. There is no `Migrations/` folder, so there is no record of schema versions to apply either. Then `SeedData` returns early if any employee exists. So once a database exists, changing the C# model never changes that database's tables. The guide's plan: add migrations, replace `EnsureCreatedAsync` with `Database.MigrateAsync`, test up/down on a copy, keep seeding idempotent.

Why the others are wrong:
- The early return skips seeding entirely; it does not reseed anything.
- A missing column is not harmless; code that uses it fails against the old table.
- `EnsureCreatedAsync` does not apply model changes to an existing database.

excerpts.quote: await db.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync(); if (await db.Employees.AnyAsync()) { return; }

No `Migrations/` folder was found. Current seeding uses `EnsureCreatedAsync` in [SeedData.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Data/SeedData.cs#L11-L11). Safe schema-change guidance: 1. Add migrations before production-like use. 2. Replace `EnsureCreatedAsync` with `Database.MigrateAsync`.

items.title: What SetNull on Department.LeadEmployee does
items.body:
`HrisDbContext` configures the department's lead with `.OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.SetNull)`. When the lead employee is deleted, the database sets the department's `LeadEmployeeId` to null instead of refusing or deleting. The department keeps existing, just without a lead until someone assigns a new one. The data-model guide: "Set null allows lead to be removed without deleting department."

Why the others are wrong:
- Refusing the delete would be `Restrict`, which is used for other relationships, not this one.
- Nothing picks a new lead automatically.
- Deleting the department too would be `Cascade`.

excerpts.quote: modelBuilder.Entity<Department>() .HasOne(d => d.LeadEmployee) .WithMany() .HasForeignKey(d => d.LeadEmployeeId) .OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.SetNull);
| Department -> LeadEmployee | [HrisDbContext.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Data/HrisDbContext.cs#L37-L41) | Set null allows lead to be removed without deleting department. |

items.title: How the critique treats the slow-search worry
items.body:
The employee search uses `ToLower().Contains`. That *might* get slow on a large table, but nobody has measured it on real data. So the critique files it under "Hypothesis", not "Confirmed": it "may become a search performance issue; measure with data before optimizing". The confirmed items, by contrast, are things anyone can check right now, like "no tests/CI/migrations/workers found". Optimising on a guess wastes effort and adds complexity; measuring first tells you whether there is a problem at all.

Why the others are wrong:
- The concern is performance, not SQL injection.
- The critique does not say SQLite indexes text automatically; it says to measure.
- It is explicitly *not* listed as confirmed.

excerpts.quote: - Confirmed: no tests/CI/migrations/workers found. - Confirmed: frontend build passes. - Hypothesis: `ToLower().Contains` may become a search performance issue; measure with data before optimizing [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L126-L133).

items.title: Why missing queues and retries are called a design boundary
items.body:
The guide searched for background-work infrastructure (hosted services, queues, outboxes, email senders, retry policies) and found none. It then says: "That is not a bug; it is a design boundary." The app simply does everything inside the request: nothing in it needs background work yet. The guide points at where the first realistic addition would go: a PTO notification after the decision is saved. Its drill designs that properly, with an outbox written in the same transaction and processed by a background service.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing is lost: approvals are saved in the request; there is just no background work.
- The guide found no background work at all, hidden or not.
- It makes no claim about production readiness; it describes a boundary of the current design.

excerpts.quote: No hosted service, queue, channel, webhook handler, email sender, retry policy, outbox, cache, or `IHttpClientFactory` usage was found. That is not a bug; it is a design boundary. The first realistic async addition would be PTO notification after [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L380-L381).

## Drill Design `PtoNotificationOutbox` as illustrative fake code. State how it is written in the same transaction as [Program.cs](../../../server/Nethris.Api/Program.cs#L380-L381), then processed by a `BackgroundService`.
